**Rule 3 (No Duplication) — the candidate**

Three guards share a literal structural template:

```
const x = <lookup>;
if (x === undefined) { throw new Error(`...`); }
return x;
```

`catalogueEntryFor`, `insuredItemOfType`, `policyAt`. That is conceptual duplication of the "a miss is a domain error" idea, repeated three times. Let me measure the extraction candidate before committing.

**APP mass — the three guards as they stand:**

`catalogueEntryFor`: bindings (item, entry) = 2; invocations (CATALOGUE index, Error ctor, throw-template interpolation of item.type) ≈ 3 → 6; conditional 1 = 4; assignment/binding-decl of entry counted as binding; constant (undefined, message literal) = 2. Roughly **14**.

Times three, plus the message literals ≈ **42** across the family. An extracted `foundOrThrow` would cost one helper (~12) plus three thin call sites (~7 each = 21) → ~33.

The mass argument favours extraction. But **Rule 2 trumps APP**, so let me test the extraction against clarity before accepting it.

content.text:
## Refactoring Complete

**File:** `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-11_09-21-32_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`

### Naming evaluation (first priority)

Checked all five guards against their current behaviour: `catalogueEntryFor`, `insuredItemOfType`, `policyAt`, `damagedAmountOf`, `overclaimedTypeIn`/`rejectOverclaimedTypes`. **No renames applied** — each already reads as what it returns, and the `overclaimedTypeIn` (returns `string | undefined`) vs. `rejectOverclaimedTypes` (throws) split correctly signals which one throws. Rule 2 was already satisfied here.

### Refactoring applied: extracted `foundOrThrow` (Rule 3)

Three of the five guards shared a literal structural template — *lookup that may miss → throw naming the offender → return the found value* — written out three times:

```ts
const foundOrThrow = <Found,>(found: Found | undefined, declined: string): Found => {
  if (found === undefined) { throw new Error(declined); }
  return found;
};
```

`catalogueEntryFor`, `insuredItemOfType`, and `policyAt` are now single expressions stating only what is looked up and what to say when it misses. The other two guards were deliberately **not** folded in: `damagedAmountOf` tests a predicate (`< 0`) rather than a miss, and `rejectOverclaimedTypes` returns void — forcing either into the helper would have been shape-matching, not shared meaning.

### APP mass

Three guards: **~42 → ~33** (helper ~12 + three call sites ~7 each). Three `if` conditionals (4 each) collapsed to one: **−8 conditional mass**.

### A judgment call worth flagging

I first wrote the message parameter as a thunk (`() => string`) for lazy evaluation. Since these are cheap interpolations, laziness bought nothing and cost a level of indirection at every call site — so I reverted it to a plain `string` (Rule 4, fewest elements).

### Note on your typecheck warning — it earned its keep

Mid-refactor I changed the signature to `string` while call sites still passed thunks. **`pnpm test` stayed fully green on all 42 tests.** Only `npx tsc --noEmit` caught it:

```
src/claim-office.ts(67,5): error TS2345: Argument of type '() => string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'
```

The reason tests missed it is worth knowing: the message argument is only touched on the throwing path, and the five error tests use loose regexes (`/amulet/`, `/sword/`, `/broomstick/`). A thunk stringifies to `"() => \`the policy does not cover...\`"` — which still *matches* `/amulet/`. So the suite would have passed while every error message shipped as source text. Those regexes can't detect message degradation; I diffed all five messages against the pre-refactor file directly and confirmed they are byte-identical.

**Final state:** 42 passing / 8 todo, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `eslint` clean.
